1410.bp: When you watch short videos on your phone, the app needs to decide which video to show you next. It tracks many signals: how long you watched, whether you liked it, whether you shared it, and so on. The goal is to learn from all these different signals at once to predict what you'll click on next, which makes the whole system more engaging and profitable.
1410.wh: The hard part is that these signals are tangled together. If you show the system just the 'watch time' signal and the 'like' signal separately, they interfere with each other—each one learned specialized knowledge that doesn't quite work well when combined. Also, as you add more and more signals, the system gets exponentially slower to train and run because it's doing redundant work for overlapping signals.
1410.ap: SCOPE splits the problem into specialized mini-experts, where each expert handles a particular kind of signal. The system then learns which experts to use for which decision, using a Transformer (a mechanism for weighing multiple pieces of information) to figure out how the different signals relate to each other. To keep experts from stepping on each other's toes, the system adds constraints that push experts to be different from one another and to stay focused on their assigned task.
1410.ww: This works because you're now training separate, focused learners that can each specialize without interference. The Transformer piece lets the system discover that, say, watch-time predictions should feed into the final ranking decision in a specific order. By explicitly penalizing redundancy, you're forcing the system to divide labor cleanly instead of all experts learning the same thing.
1410.po: On Alipay's real video platform, this approach increased user engagement by 2.47% more video views, while cutting computational cost by 43%—the system is now faster and more efficient because it's doing less wasted duplication.

1411.bp: Click prediction—guessing whether someone will click an ad or link—is one of the most important problems in online advertising and content feeds. The traditional way to solve it is to build one big model and optimize it toward a single goal. The real challenge is that after the model gets reasonably good, it plateaus and can't improve further.
1411.wh: A single model trained toward a single goal tends to get stuck in a local optimum—imagine a ball rolling downhill and getting caught in a shallow valley, never reaching the deeper valley far away. Without something pushing the model to explore different strategies, it can't escape this trap and find better solutions.
1411.ap: DPEO creates two learners instead of one, each learning slightly different strategies. They compete with each other: one becomes the 'reference' (the current best) and the other is pushed to beat it. The system keeps swapping which one is the reference and which one is trying to improve, creating an ongoing evolutionary race. The losing learner gets feedback designed to make it better than the current winner.
1411.ww: This works because competition creates pressure to explore. If you only have one model, it optimizes greedily toward immediate improvement. With two models competing, one is always being told 'you're close but not quite beating the other'—which forces it to try different approaches, escaping local traps. The role-swapping ensures neither model gets comfortable in a dead-end strategy.
1411.po: The model escapes saturation and keeps improving, with real experiments showing the system can break through performance plateaus that single-model approaches get stuck on.

1412.bp: In recent years, recommender systems have started using generative models—systems that learn to create suggestions word-by-word, like a language model. This is powerful because it can reason about complex preferences end-to-end. But there's a catch: the feedback signal from real users (clicks, purchases) is noisy and sparse, which makes the system unstable and prone to weird failure modes.
1412.wh: When you train a generative recommendation system with reinforcement learning (learning from user feedback), the sparse and noisy reward signal causes two problems. First, the system 'hacks' the reward—it learns to game metrics rather than make good recommendations, like a student memorizing test answers without understanding. Second, it drifts away from being a good language model, producing garbled or nonsensical suggestions.
1412.ap: AIPO uses two anchoring strategies. First, it cleans up the training data by identifying high-confidence user purchase signals and weighting those examples more heavily, filtering out the noisy signals that lead the system astray. Second, it adds a 'prior anchor'—a constraint that pulls the model back toward the original untrained language model, but only as strongly as needed depending on how much drift the model is experiencing.
1412.ww: Cleaning the data removes noise that causes poor learning. The prior anchor works like a penalty: it says 'stay close to the original' but doesn't enforce this uniformly—when the model is stable, the constraint is loose, but when it starts drifting badly, the constraint tightens. This balance prevents reward hacking while letting the model still improve.
1412.po: On real e-commerce datasets, AIPO produces stable training and better recommendation quality, avoiding the collapse into nonsensical or gamed suggestions that simpler approaches suffer from.

1413.bp: Converting raw text into useful question-answer pairs is valuable for building question-answering systems, search tools, and knowledge bases. Most of the world's text is unstructured (just paragraphs), so being able to automatically extract QA pairs would save enormous human effort. The challenge is doing this well at scale, especially in languages like Chinese.
1413.wh: Traditional methods either generate questions and answers separately (losing context) or do it end-to-end but are slow and can't handle ambiguity well. Building datasets for training is expensive, and systems trained on one language or domain often fail on others. There's also the hallucination problem: models invent plausible-sounding questions that don't actually match the source text.
1413.ap: The team built a large Chinese QA dataset from 143,846 documents and tested multiple language models on it. They discovered that Code Llama (a model trained on programming code and English text) actually performed better than Chinese-specialized models on Chinese text. They then created Code Llama-M by adding Chinese words to Code Llama's vocabulary, making it even better.
1413.ww: This works because Code Llama was trained on precise, structured code where accuracy matters—a misplaced semicolon breaks everything. This forces the model to be meticulous about accuracy, which transfers well to QA extraction. The extra Chinese vocabulary removes a bottleneck: Code Llama had to translate Chinese internally, wasting capacity.
1413.po: Code Llama-M produces fewer hallucinations and higher-quality QA pairs than language models built specifically for Chinese. When deployed in a real assistant system called Luo Ying, users reported meaningful satisfaction gains.

1414.bp: When an e-commerce platform sells display ad space, advertisers buy contracts guaranteeing a certain number of impressions (views) for their ads. The platform must decide which ads to show in each available slot on a webpage to satisfy all advertiser contracts while maximizing revenue. This sounds simple but becomes complex when a page has multiple ad slots.
1414.wh: Most systems treat each ad slot independently, which causes problems. Advertisers end up competing for the same slots, some contracts get fulfilled while others starve, and revenue gets concentrated in a few high-demand positions. There's no global view of what's best across all slots at once.
1414.ap: This paper formulates the problem as matching viewers and advertisers optimally across an entire page view, not slot-by-slot. The system uses a bipartite matching algorithm (pairing viewers with advertiser campaigns) and adds constraints that prevent too much exposure concentration—ensuring popular ads don't dominate all slots and less popular ads still get fair access.
1414.ww: Optimizing globally instead of locally is more efficient because you see that slot 1 and slot 2 are competing for the same valuable audience. By solving the whole matching problem at once, you can give slot 1 to the best fit and slot 2 to the second-best, rather than both going to the best (which wastes one slot). Contract roulette prevents monopolies.
1414.po: On Meituan's platform, this approach increased revenue per user by 28.99%, stabilized contract fulfillment across all advertisers (not just the biggest), and achieved better balance overall.

1415.bp: On live-streaming platforms like TikTok, the goal is to show viewers the live streams that match their interests. The system ranks streamers by predicted relevance. But there's a tension: the most popular streamers get shown to everyone, their servers get overwhelmed, and the experience suffers. Meanwhile, less-popular streamers get almost no viewers.
1415.wh: If you only optimize for relevance (matching viewers to their interests), you naturally concentrate viewers on the most popular streamers, causing server bottlenecks. The capacity constraint—that streamers can only serve so many concurrent viewers—gets ignored. Some viewers end up waiting in queues or experiencing poor video quality, and less-popular streamers never get a chance.
1415.ap: LiBRA treats the problem as a graph: viewers on one side, streamers on the other, with edges representing potential matches. The system first learns each streamer's capacity (how many viewers they can handle smoothly) using reinforcement learning. Then, a graph algorithm solves for the best matching that respects these capacity limits while still being as relevant as possible, maximizing overall viewer satisfaction globally.
1415.ww: This works because you're explicitly modeling reality: streamers have limits. Once you know those limits, you can solve for the assignment that maximizes total viewer happiness while respecting capacity, rather than greedily overfilling popular streamers. The global graph view reveals that spreading viewers more evenly actually increases total satisfaction.
1415.po: On TikTok Live, the system reduced queue times, improved stream quality for viewers who would have been on overloaded streamers, and gave less-popular streamers a fair shot at viewers who might enjoy their content.

1416.bp: On mobile e-commerce apps like Taobao, users search for products and then decide what to search for next. Predicting the next search helps the app show relevant products proactively and keep users engaged. The real-time nature (user interests change fast) and mobile constraints (phones have limited battery, memory, and network) make this tricky.
1416.wh: Sending all inference to a cloud server is slow and expensive: every user action triggers a network round-trip, adding latency and draining battery. Users' interests shift minute-by-minute as they scroll, so delayed predictions miss the window. Cloud solutions also cost a lot at scale.
1416.ap: RecGPT-Mobile runs a small language model directly on the phone. Instead of sending raw data to the cloud, the phone uses this local model to understand what the user is interested in, then sends only a compact semantic summary to the backend. The backend combines this with other signals to rank recommendations.
1416.ww: Running on-device eliminates latency: predictions happen instantly without network delay, and you get real-time adaptation as users browse. The model is small enough to fit on a phone but powerful enough to reason about semantic meaning (understanding that 'winter coat' is different from 'summer dress' without the server explaining it). This reduces data sent, lowering costs.
1416.po: Offline tests and online experiments show recommendation accuracy improved significantly. The approach is now practical for mobile devices at scale and reduces the cost of running LLM-powered systems in production.

1417.bp: E-commerce recommendation systems have traditionally used separate models for different stages (retrieval, ranking, final scoring), each optimized toward different immediate goals. This causes misalignment—earlier stages might retrieve products that later stages filter out, wasting computation. Using a single generative model end-to-end solves the misalignment but is too slow and expensive to run online.
1417.wh: Traditional multistage systems are efficient but optimize locally: each stage doesn't know what the downstream stage cares about. Generative models (like language models) can reason holistically but are too slow for real-time serving. You also need to handle very different shopping scenarios (someone browsing casually vs. searching for a gift), which generative models struggle with without separate retraining.
1417.ap: OxygenREC uses a two-speed strategy. Offline, a large language model thinks deeply (using methods like MCTS tree search) to create instructions for reasoning—summarized constraints and hints about the right kind of reasoning. Online, a smaller, fast encoder-decoder model follows these instructions to generate recommendations in milliseconds. It also learns to retrieve relevant product descriptions using a retrieval mechanism guided by these instructions.
1417.ww: This works because you offload heavy thinking to offline time. The fast online model doesn't have to rediscover reasoning from scratch; it follows the precomputed instructions, so it runs instantly. You also handle multiple scenarios with a shared backbone and scenario-specific instruction adjustments, avoiding retraining.
1417.po: On Alibaba's platform, this achieves both end-to-end semantic reasoning and practical speed, delivering measurable gains in Gross Merchandise Value and order volume across multiple shopping scenarios.

1418.bp: Understanding what users actually want to buy is the heart of e-commerce recommendation. Users have complex, evolving interests—they might want a 'blue winter coat' one day and 'blue bike accessories' the next. Capturing this complexity requires reasoning through multiple levels of abstraction: broad categories first, then specific items.
1418.wh: Earlier generative recommendation approaches do single-step prediction: they jump directly from user history to the next item. This misses the intermediate reasoning—which brands matter, which size, which color. Some use chain-of-thought (explicit reasoning steps) but lose information when translating between reasoning steps. Others do implicit reasoning but it becomes unpredictable and hard to control.
1418.ap: M2GR uses a multi-level chain-of-thought, all working in the item/product space (not abstract reasoning space). First, it predicts coarse-grained attributes in parallel: 'this user likes this brand' and 'this user likes this category' together. Then it refines these into fine-grained predictions: the exact next click item. Building on that, it predicts even more complex behavior like what the user will buy next.
1418.ww: Working entirely in item space preserves all the behavioral information—you don't lose details when translating. Coarse-first reasoning is intuitive and mirrors how humans browse: first you narrow by category, then by price, then pick the item. Parallel coarse predictions also diversify reasoning paths, creating more variety in what the system suggests.
1418.po: Online A/B tests show M2GR outperforms single-step and naive chain-of-thought approaches. The system scales to Alibaba's production infrastructure and can be added to existing recommendation pipelines without retraining.

1419.bp: Large ad platforms like Facebook retrieve candidate ads from millions, then rank them in two stages: a fast early stage and a slower, more careful final stage. This pipeline is efficient but wasteful: early stages often send ads that final ranking immediately filters out, wasting computation and latency.
1419.wh: The pipeline stages don't communicate: early ranking doesn't know what final ranking will reject, so it wastes effort sending low-value ads. Also, final ranking might see the same bad ad repeatedly from different users and reject it each time, rather than learning 'this ad is always bad' once and avoiding it upfront.
1419.ap: Cross-Stage Signal Propagation adds two-way communication. Forward: final ranking detects stable decisions (ads that consistently score low) and caches the outcome, so future low-value ads skip final ranking entirely. Backward: early ranking feeds low-value decisions back to retrieval, which then suppresses those ads at the source before they enter ranking.
1419.ww: Forward propagation eliminates redundant computation—if an ad scored terribly for 100 similar users, why compute its score again for user 101? Caching avoids recomputation. Backward propagation prevents low-value ads from wasting retrieval's time in the first place. Both work because they recognize that 'consistently bad' patterns repeat.
1419.po: On Facebook Feed, the system reduced CPU in final ranking by 10.68%, CPU in early ranking by 11.20%, and GPU by 13.01%, while keeping user and advertiser metrics stable—you're just skipping ads that weren't going to work anyway.

1420.bp: Product images, videos, and text are rich but hard to understand at scale. A recommendation system could do much better if it really understood what's in those videos and images—the style, mood, colors, objects. Multimodal language models (systems that understand both images and text) are powerful but too slow for real-time ranking at scale.
1420.wh: Traditional systems summarize multimedia as generic numerical features that miss nuance. Multimodal language models understand the content deeply but take seconds per item to run; if you have millions of items, that's infeasible. You need to extract the richness offline but make it available for fast online ranking.
1420.ap: This system uses a multimodal language model (LLaMA2 extended to handle images and video) to generate detailed captions for each product offline—describing the look, style, and context. These captions are then converted into categorical features that the recommendation model learns to use online. This separates the expensive understanding step from the fast ranking step.
1420.ww: Captions extract semantic meaning that numerical features miss (e.g., 'sleek minimalist design' vs. just pixel patterns). By running the language model once offline per item, you get rich information without real-time latency. The categorical features are fast to compute with online, so the system stays responsive.
1420.po: On real recommendation data, this approach increased offline ranking quality (AUC) by 0.35% and online user satisfaction metrics by 0.02%, showing that understanding multimedia content depth does translate to better recommendations.

1421.bp: E-commerce search is hard because product similarity depends heavily on context: a 'blue item' might be similar to another 'blue item' in clothing, but completely irrelevant in electronics. Text-based similarity often misses these category-specific nuances. The goal is to search for products that are truly similar in the way that matters for the current context.
1421.wh: Traditional embedding-based search (converting items to vectors and finding nearby vectors) treats all products the same. An algorithm might think a 'blue phone' is similar to a 'blue shirt' because both are blue, missing that the similarity metric should be different in each category. Ranking based on raw text requires processing the full product description for every candidate.
1421.ap: This approach extracts structured product attributes offline using an LLM (size, color, material, brand, etc.) organized by product category. It builds a reusable attribute graph with schemas that vary per category. At search time, instead of computing similarity over full text, the system ranks using this structured graph, reasoning about which structured attributes matter for similarity.
1421.ww: Structured attributes are efficient: instead of processing raw text for every candidate (expensive), you use precomputed attributes (fast). Category-aware schemas mean similarity metrics adapt to context: a 'size' attribute is crucial for clothing but irrelevant for electronics. The graph structure makes relationships explicit.
1421.po: Ranking precision improved by over 5% in zero-shot scenarios (no training data needed), token usage per product dropped 57%, and the approach generalizes across diverse product categories without retraining.

1422.bp: Ad platforms like eBay serve ads in two ways: keyword-targeted (advertiser picks search terms like 'blue sweater') and item-targeted (ads shown based on semantic similarity to what the user searched). Each method works but has gaps—keyword targeting needs manual setup, item-targeting fails on broad or new queries.
1422.wh: Keyword targeting requires advertisers to manually specify relevant search terms, which is labor-intensive and misses unexpected queries. Item-targeting is automatic but relies on semantic similarity, which doesn't capture all the ways an item might be relevant—a user searching 'gifts for dad' might click a power drill ad even though 'power drill' isn't semantically similar.
1422.ap: The system extracts successful query-item pairs from keyword-targeted campaigns (these clearly worked). It then uses semantic similarity to identify other similar queries that weren't in the manual list. It transfers these new query-item associations into item-targeted ads, expanding the coverage. To avoid showing irrelevant ads, it uses adaptive thresholding based on similarity confidence.
1422.ww: This works because keyword campaigns have proved the relevance: users clicked. By finding similar queries, you expand coverage without manually creating new keyword lists. Adaptive thresholding ensures you only use high-confidence associations, avoiding noisy similarity matches.
1422.po: On eBay, the approach achieved over 5% incremental impression coverage for broad and new-item queries, while maintaining click-through rate and conversion rates—expanding reach without sacrificing quality.

1423.bp: Travel recommendation systems optimize for user satisfaction and engagement, but ignore environmental impact. Popular recommendations reinforce overcrowded destinations and carbon-intensive travel. The goal is to help users make travel choices that they'll enjoy but that are also more environmentally sustainable.
1423.wh: Simply recommending 'greener alternatives' often feels preachy or restrictive to users, and they ignore it. Users also aren't always aware of the environmental impact of their choices. Traditional systems can't adapt recommendations dynamically based on a user's revealed sustainability preferences because those preferences are hidden.
1423.ap: TRACE uses a multi-agent system coordinated by an orchestrator. Different agents specialize in different tasks: one elicits sustainability preferences through conversation, one builds a detailed user persona, one generates recommendations. A key innovation is using 'counterfactual explanations'—when recommending a destination, the system also shows 'here's a similar destination that's less crowded and has lower carbon impact,' letting users see greener alternatives without being lectured.
1423.ww: Counterfactual explanations work because they invite comparison and reflection without prescription. The system surfaces the option to the user, but doesn't force it. Building a detailed persona means the system understands the user's real constraints and preferences, so recommendations stay relevant while being greener. The multi-agent design lets each component focus on its specialty.
1423.po: User studies show the system effectively supports more sustainable travel decisions while maintaining recommendation quality and conversation responsiveness. Users appreciate seeing alternatives without feeling judged.

1424.bp: Transformer-based ranking models like MonoBERT power modern search systems, deciding which documents are most relevant to a query. They work well but are black boxes: we don't understand which parts of the model drive the ranking decision. This limits our ability to debug, improve, or trust these systems.
1424.wh: Neural ranking models have millions of parameters and complex interactions. Traditional interpretability methods (like attention visualization) don't reveal the full picture because attention isn't always where the real decisions happen. To understand what's happening, you need methods that can trace how information flows through all the internal components.
1424.ap: IR Lens uses two interpretability techniques. Neuron Integrated Gradients measures how much each internal component (neurons, attention heads, layers) contributes to the final ranking decision, revealing which parts matter. Targeted ablations delete specific components and observe how predictions change, testing whether a suspected mechanism actually influences ranking.
1424.ww: Integrated Gradients work by measuring the path of gradients from output back through every component, showing which components 'light up' for different inputs. Ablations are direct: if you remove component X and ranking quality drops, X clearly matters. Together, they map the system from multiple angles.
1424.po: IR Lens provides interactive visualization of ranking decisions, enabling IR practitioners to debug models, test hypotheses about how they work, and use this understanding to improve ranking quality.
